summary: Build a mental map of cosmic scale as NESTED layers: Earth is one planet in the solar system; the Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way galaxy; and the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies in the observable universe. Two ideas carry the learning: (1) the hierarchy planet → solar system → galaxy → universe, each level containing vast numbers of the level below; and (2) a felt sense of staggering size AND emptiness, where distances dwarf the objects themselves. Across activities, keep re-locating the learner with a 'we are here' anchor, and keep scale-of-SIZE distinct from scale-of-DISTANCE.
misconceptions: Confusing the terms — using 'solar system', 'galaxy' and 'universe' interchangeably instead of as nested levels (solar system ⊂ galaxy ⊂ universe).
Thinking the Sun/solar system IS the galaxy, or that our solar system is at the centre of the galaxy or universe.
Believing the planets are close together and the solar system is crowded, underestimating how much empty space separates them.
Thinking all the stars we see at night are in other galaxies — nearly all naked-eye stars are within our own Milky Way.
Assuming the universe has a small, countable number of galaxies rather than billions.
Collapsing size and distance — imagining a scale model where planet sizes and gaps are both shrunk by the same easy-to-picture amount, missing that distances are proportionally far larger.

activities.title: Zoom out from Earth through the nested layers
steps: Starting from a view of Earth, drag or scrub a zoom control outward one step at a time: Earth shrinks to a dot as the whole solar system comes into view; the solar system collapses to a single speck of light on one arm of the Milky Way; the Milky Way dwindles to one dot in a swarm of galaxies; finally the cosmic web of light appears.
At each level, read the count shown and say it aloud: eight planets around one Sun; hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way; billions of galaxies in the universe.
Find the 'you are here' marker at every level and point to where home is before zooming further.
Watch the scale bar / 'x times bigger' counter tick upward at each jump and say what just got smaller.
activities.insight: Everything you knew — Earth, the Sun, every star you can see at night — fits inside just ONE of countless dots. The layers are nested: solar system ⊂ galaxy ⊂ universe, each containing vast numbers of the level below.

activities.title: Scale model: size versus distance
steps: Lay out (physically, with real objects, or by scrolling across a model) the Sun as a football and the planets as tiny beads at their true relative distances.
Scroll or walk across the empty gaps to reach each planet; find Earth as a lone peppercorn roughly 26 metres (an approximate anchor) from the football-sized Sun.
Say in your own words two separate things: how tiny the planets are compared with the Sun, AND how enormous the empty space between them is.
Predict before you look: are the planets crowded close together, or far apart? Then check against the model.
activities.insight: Space is mostly, staggeringly empty: the distance between planets vastly exceeds the planets' sizes. Size and distance are two different comparisons; when both are shrunk by the same factor, as in this model, the gaps turn out to be enormous compared with the objects, unlike diagrams that squeeze the gaps to fit planets on a page.

activities.title: Drill-down through the levels (discrete scaffold)
steps: Tap Earth to descend/ascend between levels: Earth → solar system → Milky Way → universe, moving one named level at a time.
At each level, reveal and read its count (8 planets / hundreds of billions of stars / billions of galaxies) and locate the 'you are here' marker.
Open a flap on the scale model that contrasts a planet's size with the gap to the next planet, and describe the contrast.
activities.insight: Each named level sits inside the next, with vast numbers at every step; the vocabulary (solar system, galaxy, universe) names distinct nested levels, not interchangeable words.

activities.title: Guided flight outward (depth view)
steps: Take a guided flight outward from Earth while layer labels appear: solar system → galaxy → local group → cosmic web.
Keep a tether or breadcrumb back to Earth in view, and point to 'we are here' as each new layer appears.
After the flight, say which layer contains which, from smallest to biggest.
activities.insight: Cosmic structure has genuine depth; flying outward can convey the three-dimensional arrangement of the nested layers and reinforce how small each level is within the next.

activities.title: Check the hierarchy and numbers
steps: Order the nested layers from smallest to biggest: planet, solar system, galaxy, universe.
Match each level to what it contains (e.g. Milky Way → hundreds of billions of stars; universe → billions of galaxies).
Answer: when you look at a star tonight, is it more likely in our own galaxy or another one? Say why.
Answer roughly how many stars are in the Milky Way and how many galaxies in the universe.
activities.insight: Confirms the hierarchy vocabulary, the headline numbers, and the fact that nearly all naked-eye stars are neighbours within our own Milky Way.

checkQuestion: Put these in order from smallest to biggest and tell me how they fit inside each other: a galaxy, the universe, a planet, the solar system. Then — the stars you see in the night sky, are they mostly in OUR galaxy, or scattered across many other galaxies? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: From smallest to biggest, nested inside each other: planet → solar system → galaxy → universe. A planet like Earth is one of several orbiting the Sun in our solar system; our solar system is one tiny part of the Milky Way galaxy, which holds billions of stars; and the Milky Way is just one of billions of galaxies in the whole universe. Almost every star you can see with your eyes at night is inside our OWN Milky Way galaxy — the other galaxies are so far away they blend into faint smudges, and only a couple can be seen at all without a telescope.
